rule: Founder, 26 November 2026: an AI may research, organize sources and draft, and never approves its own historical claims. A published museum record is existing source material that itself needs review; it is not human-approved. A claim is approved by a named human reviewer with the right expertise, then by the museum's editor for wording, uncertainty and tone. The founder approves the product and its scope and is never recorded as the historical authority. Until reviewers are named, no new historical claim is published as verified and every entry stands as 'historical review pending'.

kinds.sourced: text or a fact taken from, or linked to, a museum record: existing source material, not yet reviewed by a person
kinds.uncertain: a claim the source gives as approximate or disputed, or one the game derives from a source
kinds.reconstruction: something shown as it might have looked, with no reviewed source behind it
kinds.fiction: invented for play, and said to be on the page
kinds.convention: a way of counting or naming, not a claim

entries.claim: The game is set in the emirate of Granada under the Nasrids and is called 'The Last Kingdom of al-Andalus'; the founder's design sets it in 1475.
entries.context: Title, subtitle and the opening brief
entries.uncertainty: The title is the founder's. The year 1475 is the design's and is not stated by a museum record as a year of anything; it is a setting, not an event.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The valley, its steward, its crops, prices and seasons are invented for play.
entries.context: The note on the opening brief ('This is a game, not a history')
entries.uncertainty: None: it is said to be invented.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Eleven real places are named, each where the museum places it, and the distances between them are measured from the museum's coordinates.
entries.context: The rules' regional distances; the records linked from the brief
entries.uncertainty: The coordinates are of the places today; the distances are straight lines over the globe, not roads of the time.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The brief links the museum's records of the Alhambra, the Generalife, the Nasrid palaces, the madrasa of Granada, the Nasrid entry into Granada, the building of the Alhambra, the fall of Granada, and Ibn al-Khatib's history of Granada.
entries.context: The opening brief, 'The setting, in the museum'
entries.uncertainty: The game states nothing about them itself: it shows each record's own label and links to it.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Five ideas behind the game's mechanics are linked to museum records: market inspection, matching soil and water, improvements to the water-lifting wheel, tiraz textiles, lustreware.
entries.context: The records the game links to for the ideas behind its mechanics
entries.uncertainty: The link says the idea is real, not that the game models it faithfully. The game's numbers are invented.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The look of the valley: lime-washed houses with clay-tile roofs and shuttered openings, one with an open gallery under its roof and one with a flat roof to walk on; a town wall with a tower and a round-arched gate; a mosque with a square minaret; a watermill with a wheel; a stone bridge of three arches; ox-carts; the dress of the people who walk.
entries.context: The 3D valley
entries.uncertainty: No museum record or reviewed source stands behind any of these shapes. They are the developer's general picture of a village of the western Mediterranean and are not stated anywhere as fact; under the founder's rule of 26 November 2026 they may not be presented as the architecture or dress of Nasrid Granada until a named reviewer has seen them.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent
entries.note: First for review when a reviewer is appointed. From 26 November 2026 the houses, wall, tower and gate are models authored ahead of time (gaming/art/blender/granada_town.py), surfaced with modern photographs of plaster, tile and stone that are of no particular place or time.

entries.claim: Wheat stands ripe in late spring, olives grow on a terrace behind a broken channel, a meadow waits for water; the scenario runs ninety-six days, to the end of winter.
entries.context: The fields and the calendar
entries.uncertainty: Invented for play and covered by the note on the brief.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The valley sends wheat, olives and olive oil by cart to "the port of Málaga", which pays its own prices and offers a contract for eight measures of oil; five measures of olives press to one of oil. Prices at the village and the port move by up to fifteen parts in a hundred with what each market holds. A load takes three days to reach the port by cart.
entries.context: The Economy panel: the port, the press, the contract
entries.uncertainty: Only the port's name is real. Its prices, its buyer, the contract, the carriage, the cart limit and the pressing ratio are numbers chosen for play; the panel says they are invented. Whether naming a real port beside invented trade misleads is for a reviewer to say. The way prices move is a rule made for play, not a description of any market. Three days is a number for play, set beside the straight-line distance the museum's coordinates give (89 km); no road, pace or journey time has been taken from a source.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The steward can place a house, a granary, a cistern that lets the pool hold more water, and a walled garden with a basin and cypresses, anywhere the ground allows.
entries.context: The Construction panel's catalogue and the four buildings as drawn
entries.uncertainty: Costs, sizes, days of work and effects are numbers chosen for play. The shapes are the game's own general picture of such buildings and copy none; whether a cistern and a walled garden of these forms suit a village of this time and place is for a reviewer to say.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: In the heat of summer a village downstream asks for part of the river's flow and offers to pay; sharing brings dinars and less water, refusing costs the households' goodwill because many have kin downstream.
entries.context: The decision "The village downstream asks for water", on the objectives panel
entries.uncertainty: The village, the request, the payment and every figure are invented, and the panel says so. How water was really shared between communities on one river, and by what custom or court, is a matter of history this decision does not describe and must not be read as describing; a reviewer should say whether the framing misleads.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Granada, Málaga, Almería and the Sierra Nevada stand where the map puts them; Málaga is 89 km from Granada and Almería 109 km, in straight lines; the coast runs through Málaga, Almuñécar and Almería.
entries.context: The region card on the Overview: a diagram of positions with a scale
entries.uncertainty: The coordinates are the museum's published records, which are source material and not reviewed fact. Distances are computed from them. The coast is three points joined by straight lines and is labelled as a sketch. The game's valley is marked west of the city and is invented; the route drawn to Málaga is a straight line, not a road.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: A second year, "The Merchants of Málaga": the port offers a contract for twelve measures of oil and one for a hundred and twenty of vegetables; the steward is asked to bring in 1,600 dinars by trade, keep a contract, house eighty households and build a cistern; the village downstream asks for water again.
entries.context: The second scenario: its brief, its tasks, its contracts, its decision
entries.uncertainty: Only the port's name is real. The contracts, the buyer, the goods traded, every price and every figure are invented for play, and the brief says so. Whether vegetables were carried to a port by cart, and what a valley of this kind sold, is for a reviewer.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: A third year, "A Dry Year": little snow lies on the mountain, the river runs at about three quarters of a usual year and less rain falls; the valley is asked to hold two cisterns and to keep its households faring well for sixty days.
entries.context: The third scenario: its brief, its river, its tasks, its decision
entries.uncertainty: The year, the river's three quarters, the link drawn between snow and the river, and every figure are invented for play, and the brief says so. Whether the river of such a valley follows the mountain's snow in this way, and how communities met a dry year, is for a reviewer.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The game calls itself 'a fictional city simulation inspired by records of Abbasid Baghdad and other historical institutions of the Islamic world'; costs, yields and prices are game numbers, not historical figures.
entries.context: Help, and the note beside the museum links
entries.uncertainty: The words are the founder's. 'Inspired by' is a claim of kinship, not of accuracy: the game is not, and does not say it is, a reconstruction. Whether the kinship is fair is a reviewer's question.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Each chapter's brief quotes the museum's own account of the history behind it and links two records.
entries.context: The briefs of the three chapters
entries.uncertainty: The words quoted are the museum's summaries, unaltered; the game adds none of its own.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Each tool and building is linked to the museum's record of the real thing behind it.
entries.context: The construction tools and their descriptions
entries.uncertainty: The link says the thing is real, not that the building in the game works as it did.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Each research project is linked to a museum record.
entries.context: The research panel
entries.uncertainty: As above.

entries.claim: An endowment sets a sum aside for ever, and its yield pays a public building's upkeep: 'the game's form of the waqf'.
entries.context: Chapter 3, the Endow tool
entries.uncertainty: The principle (the principal kept, the yield given) is the museum's record; the sums and the rule that a building then costs nothing are the game's.

entries.claim: Droughts, silted canals and fevers that 'come with the caravans' strike the district.
entries.context: The events of each chapter
entries.uncertainty: Invented events in a fictional district. Under the founder's rule they are to be shown with mitigation and recovery, not as spectacle: a hospital, a granary and a cleared canal are the game's answers.

entries.claim: The look of the district: houses, domes, a bath, a library, a hospital, a water wheel.
entries.context: The 3D district
entries.uncertainty: No museum record or reviewed source stands behind these shapes. They are generic and are not stated as the architecture of Abbasid Baghdad; they may not be presented as such until reviewed.

entries.context: Every round of every day

entries.uncertainty: The game writes no statement of history of its own. Each record carries its own sources and its own uncertainty; a year or a place that is approximate in the record is approximate in the game, and the score allows for the record's precision.

entries.context: The region hint

entries.claim: The Atlas of Stories, the storm that scattered it, the ink moths, Hudhud, the Storykeeper, the workshop, its cat, its mirrors on stands and every line spoken in the scene are invented for play.
entries.context: The note under the picture and the museum note at the end ('This is a game, not a history')
entries.uncertainty: None: it is said to be invented. Since 26 November 2026 every line the scholar speaks also carries the words 'Imagined words, not a quotation' beside his name, in seven languages.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Ibn al-Haytham let light into a dark room through a small hole to test that it travels in straight lines and that a solid body cuts it; the scene's beam goes straight until a mirror turns it or the tower of books stops it.
entries.context: The puzzle's rule; the scholar's lines d_scholar_2 and d_scholar_dark_1; museum note note_2
entries.uncertainty: The record describes tests with sunlight, moonlight and lamps and a ruler; the mirrors at fixed angles on a grid are the game's own device, and the line about stopping the beam with a hand paraphrases 'cut with an opaque body'.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Until 26 November 2026 a glass prism spread the beam into colours on the Atlas page. It has been taken out of the scene.
entries.context: Formerly the prism above the reading stand and the rainbow beam; now only the museum note, which says why no prism is shown
entries.uncertainty: No museum record read for this scene says Ibn al-Haytham worked with a glass prism. It was in the scene because both of the founder's pictures for this subject show one. An independent review named it as unsupported and the founder's directive of 26 November 2026 (section 11) has it removed unless a reviewer approves a historically honest use; none has. The rule for a prism remains in the game's code, unused.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent
entries.note: Removed by the agent on the founder's directive; this is not a reviewer's decision, and the entry stays pending for one.

entries.claim: He held that light goes from the thing to the eye, against older books that had sight go out from the eye.
entries.context: The optional line d_scholar_see_1, spoken since 26 November 2026 by the Atlas's own voice as what the museum's record says, not by the scholar as his own sentence; museum note note_3
entries.uncertainty: The museum's prose attributes this to the Encyclopaedia of Islam and names Euclid, Ptolemy and al-Kindi on the other side; the game's line says only 'some old books'.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Ibn al-Haytham was born in Basra around 965 and later lived in Cairo; his best-known book is on optics.
entries.context: Museum note note_1
entries.uncertainty: The record gives the birth as 'around 354 AH/965' and notes that the reports of his death differ; the note gives no year of death.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: With the curtain drawn, the town outside appears on the workshop wall, upside down.
entries.context: The secret behind the curtain cord; lines d_secret_1 to d_secret_3
entries.uncertainty: The record read for this scene describes lights passing through one hole and falling on the wall each opposite its own source, and the museum's prose says a treatise of his sets out the dark room for watching eclipses. That a whole view appears turned over follows from the first; neither record says he described a picture of a town. Since 26 November 2026 the picture falls on the drawn curtain, which is the side opposite the hole; before that it was drawn on the back wall, which an independent review named as wrong.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The scholar's face, turban and robe, the room, the garden and the roofs through the arch.
entries.context: Everything drawn in the scene
entries.uncertainty: No portrait of Ibn al-Haytham from his own time is known to the museum; the figure follows the founder's pictures, which are themselves imaginings. The house and the skyline are composites that stand for no real building or city; clothing and architecture have not been checked for place and century.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Fifty subjects are grouped in ten worlds of five.
entries.context: The game's structure; gaming/games/hudhud/src/content/atlas.v1.json
entries.uncertainty: The grouping is a structure for play, taken from the founder's instruction; it does not say that the five of a world lived together. Each subject's own claims will be entered here when its quest is written. Three joins need a reviewer's eye first: the Sailor of Sohar (no person is named and only the port has a record), Sindbad (joined to the Thousand and One Nights, not to the museum's Book of Sindbad, which is another work) and the two thumbnail titles for al-Khwarizmi.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The player's explorer is a girl or a boy with a choice of skin, clothes and hair or headwear. The clothes are one generic tunic and vest and are the dress of no named region or century.
entries.context: The first screen and Settings; docs/gaming/hudhud/explorers.md
entries.uncertainty: Nothing on the page says where or when the clothes are from. The founder has asked for explorers from different regions over a thousand years; a roster of twelve is proposed and none is drawn, because dress by place and century must be reviewed first.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: In al-Jazari's elephant clock, every half hour figures move, a ball passes from the falcon to the dragon to a vessel with a gong and comes to rest in a bowl, and the balls gathered tell the time elapsed. One reference work dates his book of machines to 1205.
entries.context: The elephant clock quest: the order of the five parts on the ball's road, the answer to 'Ask about the balls', the museum note (gaming/games/hudhud/src/content/clock.ts; strings ck_balls_1, ck_note_2)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record, which cites the Metropolitan Museum's catalogue entry and TDV; the record itself has not been through historical review. The quest shows the parts as a row on a workbench, which no source describes.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Inside the elephant is a float with a small hole that fills and sinks in a set time; the hole was widened little by little until that time was half an hour. The bird's whistle is air pushed out by the sinking float, and a ball's weight moves the rider's arms.
entries.context: The elephant clock quest: the answer to 'Ask about the float' (ck_float_1); the bird answering to the sinking float and the rider to a ball (content/clock.ts)
entries.uncertainty: From the museum's prose on the record, after Hill's 1974 translation of al-Jazari. The game says 'half an hour' where the prose says the hole is enlarged until filling and sinking take the required time, and names half-hour timing in the next sentence: a reviewer should confirm the wording. The record warns that this establishes no rate for any copy or replica.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Each part of the clock 'answers to' one motion and 'hands on' another in a single row: the float's sinking makes the falcon let its ball go. The workbench, the muddle of parts, the apprentice and every spoken line are the game's own.
entries.context: The elephant clock quest as a whole; the museum note says so (ck_note_1, ck_note_3)
entries.uncertainty: A simplification for play. What was read for the game does not say how the falcon is made to release its ball; the record describes levers, chains, strings and pulleys inside the elephant. The apprentice is an invented, unnamed girl. Al-Jazari's one line is marked on the page as imagined words.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The opening story's frame is invented for play: a quiet museum, a great book called the Atlas of Stories, a storm that blows a window open and scatters fifty pages over ten worlds, and a hoopoe named Hudhud who lives among the museum's shelves. The fifth panel says so: 'The Atlas and the storm are invented.'
entries.context: The five panels of the opening story shown before the Atlas (pro_1 to pro_5), and the museum note on the Atlas (hub_note)
entries.uncertainty: None: it is said to be invented. The fifth panel also says the people and places behind the pages are real, or stories marked as stories; each page's own claims are entered separately.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says al-Kindi wrote the earliest treatise on breaking ciphers that survives. In it he counts the letters of a long sample of the language, ranks them from most to fewest, and compares that with the symbols of the secret message.
entries.context: The al-Kindi quest: the answer to 'Ask how to begin' and the first part of the museum note (gaming/games/hudhud/src/content/cipher.ts; strings cf_count_1, cf_note_2)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record of the method, which cites the 1987 Damascus edition of his treatise and TDV; the record itself has not been through historical review. A reviewer should check that 'earliest that survives' is the record's wording after TDV (the earliest surviving treatise, with earlier concealment acknowledged) and not 'first ever', and that 'a long sample of the language' matches the record's 'a sample of a known language'.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: He warns that a short message can mislead. And he tests a guess by looking at which letters stand side by side and at the usual openings of messages.
entries.context: The al-Kindi quest: the answer to 'Ask about short messages' and the second part of the museum note (strings cf_short_1, cf_note_2); the Challenge puzzle's short message that ranking alone gets wrong (content/cipher.ts)
entries.uncertainty: From the museum's prose on the record, after the 1987 edition. A reviewer should check the exact sense of the short-sample warning (the record says a short message may depart from ordinary usage and a guess needs checking against letter combinations and context) and that 'the usual openings of messages' is how the record puts conventional openings. The Challenge puzzle is the game's own illustration of the warning, not a case from his treatise.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The game uses drawn signs in place of Arabic letters, a page of the Atlas that the storm turned into secret marks, a fixed opening of two signs on every page (the feather, then the sun), the young messenger, and one imagined line for al-Kindi ('Do not guess. Count first, then compare.'). The three ways of playing and their rows are the game's own.
entries.context: The al-Kindi quest as a whole; the museum note says so (cf_note_1, cf_note_3, cf_note_4)
entries.uncertainty: A simplification for play. Al-Kindi worked with the letters of Arabic; the signs are the game's, so that the puzzle is the same in every language. The two-sign opening is a game rule standing in for the record's 'usual openings of messages'; the record does not say pages of any book began with a fixed opening. The messenger is an invented child. Al-Kindi's one line is marked on the page as imagined words. The note also says that the record calls the treatise the earliest that survives and does not say he invented all secret writing: a reviewer should check that this line keeps the record's limit.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says al-Khwarizmi wrote everything in words, not symbols: the unknown is a thing or a root, and the known amount is a number or dirhams. His book is named after two operations: al-jabr, restoring, which removes what is taken away on one side by adding its like to both sides; and al-muqabala, balancing, which cancels like terms on both sides.
entries.context: The al-Khwarizmi quest: the answers to 'Ask how he wrote problems' and 'Ask about the two operations', and the moves Restore and Balance (gaming/games/hudhud/src/content/algebra.ts; strings ak_words_1, ak_ops_1)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's records of the work and of algebra, which cite the Cairo 1939 edition (pp. 29-32 and the examples at pp. 69 and 121) and TDV; the records themselves have not been through historical review. A reviewer should check the glosses 'restoring' and 'balancing', the exact sense of each operation in the Cairo edition (that al-jabr adds the like of what is subtracted to both sides, and al-muqabala cancels like terms that stand on both sides), and that 'a thing or a root' and 'a number or dirhams' are the record's wording. The game's Restore and Balance moves act on whole numbers of things and of plain number and are the game's own rendering of these two sentences, not a method from the book.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: From the museum's record: al-Khwarizmi's book on al-jabr and al-muqabala brings every problem to one of six types, each with a rule and a proof by a figure. He wrote it for what people need in inheritances, trade and the measuring of land. The record says that solving equations is older than him, in Babylon, among the Greeks and in India, and that Ibn Khaldun names him as the first to write in this art.
entries.context: The al-Khwarizmi quest: the museum note at the end of the quest (strings ak_note_2, ak_note_4)
entries.uncertainty: From the museum's prose on the record, after the Cairo 1939 edition (its introduction and p. 43) and the Muqaddima as the record cites it. A reviewer should check that 'first to write in this art' is Ibn Khaldun's judgement as the record reports it and not the museum's, and that the list of older traditions is the Cairo editors' list: the record's own list is longer (it also names the Egyptian Ahmes papyrus and Heron and Diophantus), so 'Babylon, the Greeks and India' is a short form of it, and a reviewer should decide whether it needs the others.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The game uses a locked box that holds a page of the Atlas, two trays side by side with an equals sign, three problems written for play, a third move of sharing a number among things, a child who carries the box, and one imagined line for al-Khwarizmi ('Call the unknown a thing, then bring the problem to its simplest form.'). The three ways of playing and their problems are the game's own.
entries.context: The al-Khwarizmi quest as a whole; the museum note says so (strings ak_note_1, ak_note_3)
entries.uncertainty: A simplification for play. The book solves problems by rules and proofs with figures; the box, the trays, the particular problems and the step of sharing among the things are the game's, and the museum's records do not say he used trays or a pair of scales: a reviewer should check that nothing in the picture or the words implies a scale or a balance in his hands (the page's picture draws two trays and an equals sign only). The problems are of the simplest type, things equal to a number, and whole and positive, as the record says his solutions were. The child is an invented person and is named as one on the page; al-Khwarizmi's one line is marked on the page as imagined words.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says al-Idrisi wrote his book Nuzhat al-Mushtaq for Roger II, king of Sicily; by his own word in its opening he finished it in Shawwal of the year 548 of the Hijra. The museum note adds that another of the museum's records gives the year 549.
entries.context: The al-Idrisi quest: the answer to 'Ask about his book' and the first sentences of the museum note at the end of the quest (strings id_book_1, id_note_2)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's records of the person and of the work, which cite the Cairo 2002 edition (the preface, pp. 4-7) for the patron and the date; the records themselves have not been through historical review. A reviewer should check the form of Roger's title ('king of Sicily'; the preface, as the person record reports it, also names 'Italy, Ankabarda and Calabria'), and that Shawwal 548 of the Hijra is the date of the completion of the book as the author states it. The date is given in the Hijri calendar only and is not converted to a Common Era year anywhere in the game. Note for the museum's editor: another record, event/nuzhat-al-mushtaq-completed-549, gives the completion as 549 AH (1154) from a different source (a biographical encyclopedia); the two records disagree, and the game follows the person and work records, which rest on the author's own preface. The page now attributes 548 to the author's own statement and says in the museum note that another record gives 549; a reviewer should settle which the museum holds.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says the book went with a silver disc showing the seven climes, and that al-Idrisi divided each clime into ten sections, which made seventy maps.
entries.context: The al-Idrisi quest: the answer to 'Ask about the maps' and the second sentence of the museum note (strings id_maps_1, id_note_2)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's person record (which cites the Cairo 2002 edition and a TDV entry): 'to accompany the silver disc of the seven climes, dividing each clime into ten sections with seventy sectional maps'. The work record says the book comes with a world map engraved on a silver disc, in slightly different words. A reviewer should check the relation between the disc and the book (whether the disc is a map of the world, what the 'seventy sectional maps' are, and where they are kept) and the word 'clime' for the Arabic iqlim (the record's English uses both 'climes' and 'climates'). The game claims nothing more about the maps: not which way is up, not what any sheet shows, and not how the sheets were ordered or bound.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The game uses the sheets of a map lying out of order with a page of the Atlas among them, matching the edges of the sheets as the way to put them in order, an imagined coast drawn from the edge codes, a young helper who dropped the sheets, and one imagined line for al-Idrisi ('Look at the edges of the sheets: a coast or a river does not stop at the edge.'). The three maps and their edges are the game's own: six, twelve or fifteen sheets, not seventy.
entries.context: The al-Idrisi quest as a whole; the museum note says so (strings id_note_1, id_note_3, id_intro_2)
entries.uncertainty: A simplification for play. Nothing read for the game says how al-Idrisi's maps were ordered, bound, oriented or what any sheet showed. A reviewer should check that nothing in the picture can be mistaken for his map or for a real coast (the lines on every sheet are generated from small edge codes by code, and the three maps were written for the game; none is traced from any map or coastline), and that the imagined line about a coast or a river at an edge claims nothing about his practice. The young helper is an invented person and is named as one on the page; al-Idrisi's one line is marked on the page as imagined words.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says al-Jahiz divided animals in his book by how they move: those that walk, fly, swim or creep, the walkers being humans, beasts, predators and vermin; and that in this he follows the names established and known among the people of his language.
entries.context: The al-Jahiz quest: the answer to 'Ask about his division of animals' and the first sentence of the museum note at the end of the quest (strings jz_divide_1, jz_note_2)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record of the work (the section 'The division of beings'), which cites the Beirut 2003 edition, vol. 1 pp. 24 to 25; the record itself has not been through historical review. A reviewer should check the Arabic terms for the four ways of moving: the game writes the verb for 'creep' as يزحف, and the edition may use another word, or another order. A reviewer should also check that 'the names established and known among the people of his language' is his own statement about this division, as the record says (p. 25), and not a general claim about his method. The game gives no date and says nothing more about the book's structure here.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says that al-Jahiz divides birds into predators, grazers and swarming insects; tells predators armed with talons, such as the eagle, from those armed with beaks, such as vultures and crows; and notes that not everything that flies on two wings is a bird: locusts, bees and flies fly but are not called birds, the bat is reckoned among birds though featherless, and the ostrich has feathers but is not a bird. It lists the hoopoe among the creatures treated in the third part of the book, and its editor says the book holds far more than its title suggests.
entries.context: The al-Jahiz quest: the answers to 'Ask about the birds' and the hoopoe lines that follow the second question, and the second and fourth paragraphs of the museum note (strings jz_birds_1, jz_hoopoe_1, jz_note_2, jz_note_4)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record of the work, which cites the Beirut 2003 edition, vol. 1 pp. 25 to 27 for the birds, vol. 2 pp. 3 and 509 for the hoopoe, and vol. 1 pp. 4 to 5 for the editor's remark; the record itself has not been through historical review. A reviewer should check each example against pp. 25 to 27 of the cited edition, and in particular whether vultures and crows are his examples for beaks and the eagle his example for talons, as the record says. For the museum's editor: an earlier draft of the hoopoe line said 'the second part'; the record's chapter list puts the hoopoe in the third part, which opens volume 2, and the game says the third part. A reviewer should confirm which part the edition's own list gives it. The English 'bird' stands for the edition's Arabic word, and the game does not claim how he used it elsewhere; it claims no more than these sentences.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The game uses animal cards and trays, and putting cards in the trays, as the way to play his division; three groupings as the game words them (Story: called a bird or not; Explorer: counted among the birds or not, the game's summary of his statements; Challenge: five phrases of the passage); simple code-drawn pictures of eight animals; a girl who carries the cards; one imagined line for al-Jahiz ('Do not judge by feathers or by wings alone. See what people call each one.'); and a sentence that science today counts the bat among the mammals and the ostrich among the birds, which is general knowledge and not taken from the record.
entries.context: The al-Jahiz quest as a whole; the museum note says so (strings jz_note_1, jz_note_3, jz_intro_2 and the group names jz_g_*)
entries.uncertainty: A simplification for play. Nothing read for the game says that al-Jahiz sorted anything into trays or into these groupings. Explorer's two-way split is the game's summary of several of his statements, not his own division, and each Challenge phrase is the game's wording of a statement in the passage. A reviewer should check that each phrase stays within what the record says; that the drawings, which are simple and made in code, cannot be taken for a claim about how any animal looks; and, above all, whether a child could take his division for present-day biology despite the museum note, which says that science sorts animals in another way. The sentence about today's science is general knowledge and has no source in the record; a reviewer should decide whether it may stand. The girl is an invented person and is named as one on the page; al-Jahiz's one line is marked on the page as imagined words.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says that transmitted accounts tell that Chinese artisans captured in a battle near the Talas river in 751 taught the people of Samarkand to make paper from linen and hemp rags, and that this is a report handed down, not a proved beginning (a transmitted account rather than a proved foundation act). It also says that the Chinese invented paper and that the part of the Islamic world was to receive the craft, adapt it and spread it.
entries.context: The paper-of-Samarkand quest: the answer to 'Ask about the old report' and the first two sentences of the museum note at the end of the quest (strings pp_story_1, pp_note_2)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record of the invention (its summary, 'The story' and 'Who invented it?'), after the Encyclopaedia of Islam and Carter 1925; the record itself has not been through historical review, and it says the prisoner story was transmitted by al-Tha'alibi two centuries later, that the Tang annals confirm the battle's date and not the papermakers' presence, and that Carter notes the Arabic report's 'grasses and plants' against the surviving rag papers. A reviewer should check that the game's sentence keeps the report a report ('an old report tells', 'a report handed down, not a proved beginning') and that nothing else on the page, in any of the seven languages, states it as fact. The record gives the date as 133-134/751 (its two Encyclopaedia of Islam articles differ by a year); the game gives 751 only and adds no Hijri year, and a reviewer should decide whether that is enough. The record's summary says 'linen and hemp rags' and its recipe sentence 'linen, flax or hemp rags'; the game says 'linen or hemp', and a reviewer may want flax named. Other museum records do not say the same: place/samarqand says flatly that paper was 'brought in by the Chinese artisans captured at the battle of Talas in 133/751', with none of the record's caution (the game follows the invention record); content/en/job/papermaker.md, after the TDV entry, says that some researchers put the start in Samarkand with the captives of Talas in 756 and that the Iranica assessment differs; and invention/baghdad-papermaking reports, through Bloom's Iranica article, a Manichaean community producing paper for export in Samarkand from the Hudud al-Alam. The game says none of these things. A reviewer should decide whether the sentence should say that dates and origins differ between sources, and whether the Chinese invention of paper is stated at the right strength.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record gives the way paper was made: rags of linen or hemp are cut small, cleaned and bleached, pounded in water to a pulp and dressed with wheat starch, lifted on a mould and shaken until the fibres hold together; the sheet is laid flat and dried on a wall, then rubbed with flour and starch and polished smooth. For the pounding it names mortars, stampers and paper-mills. From Samarkand the craft moved to Baghdad, and on to Egypt, Damascus, the Maghrib, Jativa in Spain and other lands.
entries.context: The paper-of-Samarkand quest: the order of the steps that is the answer in all three ways of playing, the step sentences shown as a run is made, the answer to 'Ask how paper was made', and the second and third paragraphs of the museum note (content/paper.ts; strings pp_how_1, pp_did_*, pp_part_*, pp_note_2, pp_note_3)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record of the invention ('What it is', 'How it works' and 'The spread'), which cites the Encyclopaedia of Islam, vol. IV pp. 440-441 for the recipe and vol. IV p. 440 and Carter pp. 98-99 for the spread; the record itself has not been through historical review. The order is joined from two sentences of the record: one lists the rags cut small, cleaned, bleached and pounded, then dressed with wheat-starch size and drawn through a deckle; the other says the fibres are pounded to pulp, dressed with starch, lifted on a deckle and shaken until they interlace, and the sheet is laid flat, dried on a wall, rubbed with flour-and-starch and polished smooth. A reviewer should check that this is one order and that cleaning comes before bleaching as the list has it (Challenge makes them two cards in that order). A reviewer should also check that the recipe in the record is a general description of the craft and that the game does not date it to 751 or tie it to Samarkand alone: the game says 'the record gives the way it was made' and gives no date to the recipe. The words differ a little from the record's: the record says 'rotten' where the game says 'worn-out' for the rags, 'deckle' where the game says 'mould', and 'wheat-starch size' where the game says 'dressed with wheat starch'. For the spread the record names Baghdad first and then the Tihama, Yemen, Egypt, Damascus, Tripoli, Hama, Manbij, Tiberias, the Maghrib, Jativa, Persia and India; the game names five and says 'and other lands', and the record warns that this does not make every later mill a direct branch of Samarkand, so a reviewer should check that 'moved to Baghdad, and on to' is not read as a single line (invention/baghdad-papermaking says Baghdad's background is the movement of paper and skills through Central Asia, Samarkand included).
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The game uses a papermaker's workshop in which a page of the Atlas, torn in a storm, is remade; a papermaker and a child who helps, both invented people; one card for each step (and, in Story and Explorer, one card where the record's own sentence joins two or three steps); a row of places in which the cards are put in order, with what each step does to the material said and drawn (scraps, pulp, a sheet); a single mallet for the record's mortars, stampers and paper-mills; and simple pictures of each step drawn in code.
entries.context: The paper-of-Samarkand quest as a whole; the museum note says so (strings pp_note_1, pp_note_3, pp_intro_1, pp_intro_2, pp_part_*, pp_kind_*, pp_who_*)
entries.uncertainty: A simplification for play. Nothing read for the game says that any papermaker kept cards of steps, that a workshop at Samarkand looked as drawn, or that paper was made in exactly these five, seven or eight separate stages; the joining of steps in Story is the game's. A reviewer should check that the drawings, which are simple and made in code, cannot be taken for a claim about how a tool or a vat looked, and that the single mallet does not read as the record's only means of pounding (the note says it is one mallet for mortars, stampers and mills). A reviewer should also check that the invented papermaker, who is named on the page as an invented person, is not mistaken for a named historical person: the record says that no papermaker's name survives and gives credit to transmitters (Ziyad ibn Salih in the account); the game names no one.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says Ibn Battuta left Tangier on Thursday the second of Rajab in the year 725 of the Hijra for the pilgrimage, alone, aged twenty-two. It also says he did not write his journey down himself: Sultan Abu Inan ordered it written, Ibn Battuta dictated it, and Ibn Juzayy edited it.
entries.context: The Ibn Battuta quest: the answers to 'Ask when he set out' and 'Ask who wrote his journey down' (strings ib_left_1, ib_written_1)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record of the person ('Overview', 'In the Khayriyya edition of the Rihla' and 'How the Rihla Was Written'), which gives the day, the Hijri date, the purpose, 'alone' and the age from the Rihla's own opening (Khayriyya edition, p. 15, as the record cites it) and who ordered, dictated and edited the account from the Rihla's preface and the Encyclopaedia of Islam (vol. 3 p. 768); the record itself has not been through historical review. A reviewer should check the weekday and the age against the Rihla's own opening. The record's own dates are 17 Rajab 703 for his birth and 2 Rajab 725 for his leaving, which is about a fortnight short of twenty-two years, so 'aged twenty-two' is the Rihla's own count and not a count from the record's dates; another museum record, event/ibn-battuta-sets-out-for-hajj-1325 (after Britannica), says 'aged 21' and gives only the year 1325. The game follows the person record and does not say how the age was counted. The record's Encyclopaedia of Islam paragraph converts 2 Rajab 725 to 13 June 1325, which is a Thursday in the Julian calendar, and the game gives no Gregorian date. For the account, the record says in one place that the sultan ordered it written down, that he dictated it and that Ibn Juzayy edited it, and in another that the article stresses it was 'not written down by Ibn Battuta himself but by a scholar, Ibn Juzayy, commissioned by' Abu Inan: the game says 'ordered it written, dictated it, edited it' and does not say whether Ibn Juzayy is the one who wrote it down from dictation. A reviewer should decide whether 'edited' is the right word beside the article's 'written down'. The game gives no date for the finishing of the account, on which museum records differ: the person record says 3 Dhu al-Hijja 756 and, in the article's paragraph, 9 December 1357, while work/rihla-ibn-battuta derives December 1355 from the same Hijri day; and event/ibn-battuta-dictates-rihla-1353 places the dictation 'towards the end of 1353'.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says an Encyclopaedia of Islam article sets out Ibn Battuta's journeys in eight stages and warns that some details remain uncertain. The game follows three of them as a road to be threaded: the first (Tangier, North Africa, Egypt, Upper Egypt and Syria, then Damascus for Mecca), the second (from Mecca through Iraq, Khuzistan, Fars and the Jibal, then Tabriz, Baghdad, Samarra and Mosul, returning to Baghdad) and the third (down the Red Sea to Yemen and Aden, then Zayla, Mogadishu and the trading ports of East Africa, and back by Oman and the Persian Gulf). The record also says that Ibn Battuta admitted he had sometimes lost his notes and rewritten them from memory, that the article holds the rearranging of several itineraries comes from the editor, and that these weaknesses do not detract from the value of the whole.
entries.context: The Ibn Battuta quest: the three roads and which way of playing follows which (Story the first stage, Challenge the second, Explorer the third), the three sentences shown as the stage's text, and the second and third notes at the end (content/route.ts; strings ib_stage_story, ib_stage_explorer, ib_stage_challenge, ib_note_2, ib_note_3, ib_stop_*)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record of the person ('The Eight Stages of His Journeys', 'How the Rihla Was Written' and 'The Text and the Question of Reliability'), all after one article of the Encyclopaedia of Islam (vol. 3 pp. 767-768); the record itself has not been through historical review. The article warns that some details of the chronology remain uncertain, and the game does not say which. A reviewer should check each stop's place in its stage against the article. In particular: that Egypt and Upper Egypt are two stops of the first stage; that Baghdad comes twice in the second (once among 'Tabriz, Baghdad, Samarra and Mosul' and once as 'returning to Baghdad'); and that the third stage lists Zayla, Mogadishu and 'the trading ports of East Africa' as the record does, where the game's bead for the ports is the game's own plain name. The work record's structure line for the Rihla (part 1) also names Tunis, Alexandria, Cairo and Medina on the way to Mecca, which the article's sentence for the first stage does not, and puts Oman and the Gulf after the East African coast, as the third stage does; the game follows the article's sentences and says so. The game leaves out what the article adds to the second stage (a stay in Arabia with three pilgrimages, from 727 to 730) and to the third (a further pilgrimage in 732). A reviewer should also decide whether presenting an itinerary as a fixed order to be learned misleads, given the record's caution that the editor rearranged several itineraries and that Ibn Battuta rewrote lost notes from memory: the third note says 'the order here is the order of the account as that article sets it out', which is not the same as the order he travelled, and the game does not say which itineraries were rearranged. The record's separate question page (question/credibility-of-ibn-battuta) is about another matter, the doubts about his tales of India, and the game links it as further reading and does not state its content. The Arabic sentence of the third stage says 'the Gulf' with no adjective, on purpose; the English follows the record in 'the Persian Gulf'. The museum's own records and pages name that sea in more than one way (its place record is 'الخليج العربي' in Arabic and 'Persian Gulf' in English, 'Arap Körfezi' in Turkish and 'Teluk Arab' in Indonesian, and its pages use both the Persian and the Arabian forms in several languages), and the game's other languages follow the commonest form in each language's museum pages, which a reviewer should confirm is acceptable.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The game uses a thread and a set of beads, one for each stop of a stage, set round a ring that is not a map; small signs and dots on the beads to tell them apart; a child with a camel, an invented person, who is answered kindly or bluntly; one line spoken by Ibn Battuta in imagined words ('A road is remembered by its order: where you set out, and then where next.'); and a choice of three stages out of the record's eight, played in three ways.
entries.context: The Ibn Battuta quest as a whole; the first note says so (strings ib_note_1, ib_intro_1, ib_intro_2, ib_who_*, ib_child_*, ib_picture; art/route.ts)
entries.uncertainty: A simplification for play. Nothing read for the game says that Ibn Battuta or any traveller kept the order of a road by beads on a thread, that he said what the game's line says, or that a child with a camel was met on his road; the line and the child are invented and the page says so (the speakers' labels read 'in imagined words' and 'an invented person'). A reviewer should check that the ring cannot be read as geography: the beads sit in an order that is never the road's, no direction or distance is drawn, no coast, compass or place is drawn, the thread's straight lines cross the ring and mean only 'next', and the picture's alt text and the first note say the picture is not a map. A reviewer should also check that the choice of three stages out of eight (the first, the second and the third, played as Story, Challenge and Explorer) is not read as a claim that these were his most important journeys, that he went nowhere else (the other five stages, which reach India, the Maldives, China, Sumatra, Granada and the Niger, are not played), or that they were separate journeys: the record calls them stages of his journeys. Where a stop has a museum place record the game takes its name from that record's label in each language, with the exceptions listed in the pull request (a bracketed gloss dropped, an article added, a wrong word for the place replaced by the form the museum's pages use, or the form the stage's sentence uses); a reviewer should check that no name reads as a claim.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent
